correctness.rationale: The recurrence can be reconstructed exactly stage by stage because every attainable sum is finite and its least prime factor can be computed deterministically. Independent replay reproduced all published cardinalities through generation 27, verified \(Q_n=M_n\) for every \(1\le n\le26\), and obtained \(|C_{26}|=105412\), \(M_{26}=162143\), \(|C_{27}|=170224\), \(M_{27}=262331\), \(R_{27}=262321\), \(Q_{27}=262313\). The positive maximum witness \(100188+162143=262331\) uses two elements of \(C_{26}\). Since \(2M_{26}<2R_{27}\), a composite sum cannot map to \(R_{27}\); exact pair-sum exclusion therefore certifies its absence. The computation is exhaustive integer arithmetic, not sampling.

value.rationale: The maximum and complete-prime frontier are central quantities in the recent asymptotic theory. Locating their first exact separation is a natural finite boundary that complements the asymptotic theorem and is supported by a complete stage-by-stage certificate.

final_claim: For Conway's subprime closure, every prime up to the stage maximum is present through generation \(26\), while generation \(27\) is the first failure: \(|C_{27}|=170224\), \(M_{27}=262331\), the least missing prime is \(R_{27}=262321\), and its predecessor is \(Q_{27}=262313\).
limitations: This is an exact finite boundary through generation \(27\); it gives no frequency law for later prime-prefix gaps.
The exhaustive computation is tied to the stated Conway subprime recurrence.
